claims.source: Another report provided evidence of a periosteum-resident Mx1+αSMA+ stem cell subpopulation that expressed chemokine CCL receptors needed for effective bone healing (Ortinau et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Ortinau et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Insufficient bone fracture repair represents a major clinical and societal burden.
claims.source: Insufficient bone fracture repair represents a major clinical and societal burden and novel strategies are needed to address it.
claims.evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge about fracture healing complications.

claims.claim: About 5–10% of patients experience healing deficiencies leading to problematic and costly non-unions.
claims.source: These discoveries would also hold high clinical significance and importance as such knowledge could be leveraged to mitigate healing deficiencies seen in about 5–10% of patients, leading to problematic and costly non-unions that are not fully addressed by current therapeutic strategies (Hak et al., 2014; Tzioupis and Giannoudis, 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hak et al., 2014 and Tzioupis and Giannoudis, 2007.

claims.claim: Current therapeutic strategies do not fully address fracture non-unions.
claims.source: These discoveries would also hold high clinical significance and importance as such knowledge could be leveraged to mitigate healing deficiencies seen in about 5–10% of patients, leading to problematic and costly non-unions that are not fully addressed by current therapeutic strategies (Hak et al., 2014; Tzioupis and Giannoudis, 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hak et al., 2014 and Tzioupis and Giannoudis, 2007.

claims.claim: Activin A has a role in promoting heterotopic ossification (HO) in mice.
claims.source: Recent studies from our laboratories and others have revealed that the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) superfamily member Activin A has a previously unsuspected role in promoting HO in mice (Hatsell et al., 2015; Hino et al., 2015; Mundy et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hatsell et al., 2015; Hino et al., 2015; Mundy et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Activin A is produced by activated macrophages and regulates cytokine production and profile.
claims.source: This protein is best known for its roles in inflammation where it is produced by activated macrophages and regulates cytokine production and profile (de Kretser et al., 2012; Morianos et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to de Kretser et al., 2012 and Morianos et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Activin A has pro-chondrogenic activity on human and mouse progenitor cells.
claims.source: The protein has also been found to have pro-chondrogenic activity on human and mouse progenitor cells (Mundy et al., 2021; Djouad et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mundy et al., 2021 and Djouad et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Td+ cells in Col2a1-Cre;Gt(Rosa)26 tdTomato mice are major contributors to fracture callus.
claims.source: Here, we selected Col2a1-Cre;Gt(Rosa)26 tdTomato (Col2/Td) reporter mice because as our previous study indicated, Td+ cells in these mice are major contributors to fracture callus (Wang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019 and by spatiotemporal analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In intact tibiae, the cortical bone surface was covered by a thin layer of periosteum mainly consisting of Td+ cells.
claims.source: In intact tibiae, the cortical bone surface was covered by a thin layer of periosteum mainly consisting of Td+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Aa, Ba).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: At day 5 post fracture, Td+ cells had greatly expanded in number to form the thickened periosteum.
claims.source: At day 5 post fracture, Td+ cells had greatly expanded in number to form the thickened periosteum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Ab, Bb).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: By day 10, all chondrocytes as well as neighboring fibrotic cells were Td+.
claims.source: By day 10 when cartilage reached its peak soft callus development as shown by Safranin O staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Bc), all chondrocytes as well as neighboring fibrotic cells were Td+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Ac).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence and histological images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: By day 15, Td+ cells constituted the majority of osteoblasts and osteocytes in the callus.
claims.source: By day 15 when most cartilage was undergoing endochondral ossification, Td+ cells now constituted the majority of osteoblasts and osteocytes in the callus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Ad, Bd).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence and histological images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the remodeling bone present by day 30, the new periosteum at the edge of callus mostly consisted of Td+ cells.
claims.source: In the remodeling bone present by day 30, the new periosteum at the edge of callus mostly consisted of Td+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Ae, Be).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence and histological images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Td+ cells, but not Td− cells, were able to form cell colonies in CFU-F assays of periosteal cells isolated from intact bones.
claims.source: Colony-forming unit fibroblast (CFU-F) assays of periosteal cells isolated from intact bones revealed that Td+ cells, but not Td− cells, were able to form cell colonies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: Supported by CFU-F assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: The percentage of Td+ cells among freshly isolated periosteal cells increased from 2.8% at day 0 to 3.4% at day 5 and 8.5% at day 10.
claims.source: The percentage of Td+ cells among freshly isolated cells increased from 2.8% at day 0 to 3.4% at day 5 and 8.5% at day 10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: 7,496, 7,535, and 10,398 Td+ cells were sequenced from days 0, 5, and 10 samples, respectively, with a median of 3,462 genes/cell and 13,463 UMIs/cells.
claims.source: Using the 10× Genomics approach, we sequenced 7,496, 7,535, and 10,398 Td+ cells from days 0, 5, and 10 samples, respectively, with a median of 3,462 genes/cell and 13,463 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs)/cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq quality control data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The merged scRNA-seq dataset comprising 25,429 cells resolved into 16 cell clusters.
claims.source: We merged the resulting three datasets comprising an overall total of 25,429 cells that resolved into 16 cell clusters, including 6 clusters of periosteal mesenchymal lineage cells, 4 clusters of hematopoietic cells, 1 cluster of muscle cells, 1 cluster of synovial lining cells, 1 cluster of tendon cells, 1 cluster of endothelial cells (ECs), 1 cluster of Schwann cells, and 1 cluster of smooth muscle cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D; Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: Supported by UMAP plots and cluster identification in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D.

claims.claim: Td expression was detected in all clusters but was highest in mesenchymal cells.
claims.source: Td expression was detected in all clusters but was highest in mesenchymal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by expression pattern shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: After removing non-mesenchymal cells, the recalculated data identified six distinct mesenchymal cell clusters.
claims.source: Given the focus of our study on mesenchymal lineage cells in callus, we digitally removed those clusters as well as other non-mesenchymal cells. As a result, the recalculated data identified six distinct mesenchymal cell clusters (Figure 2A, B; Supplementary file 1b).
claims.evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 2A and B showing six mesenchymal clusters.

claims.claim: Clusters 3, 4, 5, and 6 represented early osteoblasts (EOB), osteoblasts (OB), chondrocytes (CH), and hypertrophic chondrocytes (HCH), respectively.
claims.source: Based on lineage-specific traits, clusters 3, 4, 5, and 6 represented early osteoblasts (EOB), osteoblasts (OB), chondrocytes (CH), and hypertrophic chondrocytes (HCH), respectively (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by violin plots of cluster-specific markers in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Cells in cluster 1 were characterized by typical stem cell markers such as Cd34, Ly6a (Sca1), and Thy1 (Cd90), suggesting they represented mesenchymal progenitor cells (MPCs).
claims.source: Cells in cluster 1 were characterized by several typical stem cell markers such as Cd34, Ly6a (Sca1), and Thy1 (Cd90), suggesting that they represented mesenchymal progenitor cells (MPCs).
claims.evidence: Supported by violin plots in Figure 2C showing expression of stem cell markers in cluster 1.

claims.claim: Cluster 2 cells markedly increased in number early from days 0 to 5.
claims.source: When the merged datasets (Figure 2A) were separated by time point, it became clear that cluster 2 cells markedly increased in number early from days 0 to 5
claims.evidence: Supported by UMAP plots separated by time point in Figure 2B and cell number estimates in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Chondrocytes (cluster 5), hypertrophic chondrocytes (cluster 6), and osteoblasts (clusters 3 and 4) expanded by day 10.
claims.source: When the merged datasets (Figure 2A) were separated by time point, it became clear that cluster 2 cells markedly increased in number early from days 0 to 5, whereas chondrocytes (cluster 5), hypertrophic chondrocytes (cluster 6), and osteoblasts (clusters 3 and 4) expanded by day 10 (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 2B and cell number estimates in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Cluster 2 contained highly proliferative cells, particularly at day 5.
claims.source: Interestingly, computational cell cycle analysis revealed that cluster 2 contained highly proliferative cells, particularly at day 5 (Figure 2D, E).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: Several proliferation marker genes, such as Ccnd3, Cdk4, Cdc20, Cdca3, Mcm4, and Cepna, were highly expressed in cluster 2 at the day 5 time point.
claims.source: Several proliferation marker genes, such as Ccnd3, Cdk4, Cdc20, Cdca3, Mcm4, and Cepna, were highly expressed in cluster 2 at the day 5 time point (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by violin plots of proliferation markers in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: RNA velocity analysis showed that directionality of cell differentiation and diversification started from cluster 1 (MPCs), advanced through cluster 2 (PPCs) and ended in cluster 4 (OBs) and cluster 6 (HCH).
claims.source: Applying this approach to our merged datasets above (Figure 2A), we found that directionality of cell differentiation and diversification started from cluster 1 (MPCs), advanced and transitioned through cluster 2 (PPCs) and ended in cluster 4 (OBs) and cluster 6 (HCH) (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: Pseudotemporal cell trajectory analysis placed MPC cells at one end of the developmental trajectory, PPC cells in a central position, and OBs and CHs at the other two ends.
claims.source: Likewise, at every time point, pseudotemporal cell trajectory analysis placed MPC cells (cluster 1) at one end of the developmental trajectory, PPC cells (cluster 2) in a central position, and OBs (cluster 4) and CHs (clusters 5 and 6) at the other two ends (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Slingshot trajectory plots in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: MPCs serve as stem/progenitors and give rise to PPCs which in turn diverge into chondrocytes and osteoblasts.
claims.source: Together, the data strongly indicate that MPCs serve as stem/progenitors and give rise to PPCs which in turn diverge into chondrocytes and osteoblasts, contributing to soft and hard callus formation.
claims.evidence: Based on integration of trajectory analysis, RNA velocity, and cell cycle data showing developmental relationships between cell clusters.

claims.claim: The most up-regulated genes in PPCs indicated their myofibroblast-like phenotype.
claims.source: In the merged dataset, the most up-regulated genes in PPCs indicated their myofibroblast-like phenotype.
claims.evidence: Supported by GO term analysis in Figure 3A and expression of myofibroblast marker genes in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Up-regulated genes in PPCs were closely related to processes and pathways known to be regulated by myofibroblasts such as wound healing, focal adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, and contractile actin filament.
claims.source: Those genes were closely related to processes and pathways known to be regulated by myofibroblasts such as wound healing, focal adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, and contractile actin filament (Hsia et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: Supported by GO term analysis in Figure 3A and citation to Hsia et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Known myofibroblast marker genes such as Acta2, Tagln, Tagln2, Myl9, Actg1, Tpm2, and Fbn2 were up-regulated in PPCs.
claims.source: Those genes were closely related to processes and pathways known to be regulated by myofibroblasts such as wound healing, focal adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, and contractile actin filament (Hsia et al., 2016), and included known myofibroblast marker genes such as Acta2, Tagln, Tagln2, Myl9, Actg1, Tpm2, and Fbn2 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Hsia et al., 2016; López-Antona et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by violin plots in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and citations to Hsia et al., 2016 and López-Antona et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The expression of myofibroblast marker genes was highly up-regulated at day 5 and then reduced at day 10.
claims.source: The expression of these genes was highly up-regulated at day 5 and then reduced at day 10 (Figure 3B)
claims.evidence: Supported by violin plots showing temporal expression patterns in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Fracture transiently promotes PPCs into a myofibroblast-like phenotype.
claims.source: The expression of these genes was highly up-regulated at day 5 and then reduced at day 10 (Figure 3B), suggesting that fracture transiently promotes PPCs into a myofibroblast-like phenotype.
claims.evidence: Based on temporal expression patterns of myofibroblast markers shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The least expressed genes in PPCs were those related to bone mineralization and chondrocyte differentiation.
claims.source: Conversely, the least expressed genes were those related to bone mineralization and chondrocyte differentiation, confirming that the PPCs did not possess a terminally differentiated phenotype (Figure 3A, B).
claims.evidence: Supported by GO term analysis in Figure 3A showing down-regulated pathways in PPCs.

claims.claim: Compared to MPCs, PPCs highly expressed Inhba after fracture.
claims.source: Particularly relevant to the present study was the finding that compared to MPCs, PPCs highly expressed Inhba after fracture (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by violin plots in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing Inhba expression patterns.

claims.claim: Chondrocytes highly expressed Inhba, consistent with immunostaining results.
claims.source: Note that chondrocytes also highly expressed Inhba, consistent with the immunostaining results shown in Figure 1.
claims.evidence: Supported by violin plots in Figure 3C and immunostaining in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The number of chondrocytes was much lower than PPCs in early callus.
claims.source: However, their number was much lower than PPCs in early callus (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B)
claims.evidence: Supported by cell number estimates in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: PPCs are likely to be the main source of Activin A in early fracture healing.
claims.source: However, their number was much lower than PPCs in early callus (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), suggesting that PPCs are likely to be the main source of Activin A in early fracture healing.
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of cell numbers and Inhba expression levels between PPCs and chondrocytes.

claims.claim: Activin A binds to type II receptors (ActRIIA or ActRIIB) to recruit and phosphorylate type I receptors (ALK4 or ALK7) for initiating its intracellular signaling.
claims.source: Activin A binds to type II receptors (ActRIIA or ActRIIB) to recruit and phosphorylate type I receptors (ALK4 or ALK7) for initiating its intracellular signaling (Pangas and Woodruff, 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Pangas and Woodruff, 2000, representing established knowledge about Activin A signaling.

claims.claim: Genes encoding Activin A receptors (Acvr2a, Acvr2b, Acvr1b, and Acvr1c) were expressed in all mesenchymal progenitor populations.
claims.source: uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plots suggested that genes encoding these receptors (Acvr2a, Acvr2b, Acvr1b, and Acvr1c, respectively) were expressed in all mesenchymal progenitor populations
claims.evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing receptor expression patterns.

claims.claim: Acvr2a expression was enriched in MPCs.
claims.source: uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plots suggested that genes encoding these receptors (Acvr2a, Acvr2b, Acvr1b, and Acvr1c, respectively) were expressed in all mesenchymal progenitor populations and Acvr2a expression was enriched in MPCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing Acvr2a expression pattern.

claims.claim: MPCs were less proliferative than PPCs at both days 0 and 5.
claims.source: EdU incorporation indicated that MPCs were less proliferative than PPCs at both days 0 and 5, though bone fracture did enhance proliferation in both populations (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation flow cytometry data in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Bone fracture enhanced proliferation in both MPCs and PPCs.
claims.source: EdU incorporation indicated that MPCs were less proliferative than PPCs at both days 0 and 5, though bone fracture did enhance proliferation in both populations (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation flow cytometry data in Figure 3D comparing day 0 and day 5.

claims.claim: Cd34+ cells highly expressed MPC markers including Cd34, Ly6a, Cd248, and Clec3b.
claims.source: In addition, quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis of cells sorted from day 5 callus verified that Cd34+ cells highly expressed MPC markers including Cd34, Ly6a, Cd248, and Clec3b
claims.evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3E showing expression of stem cell markers in sorted Cd34+ cells.

claims.claim: Cd34− cells more strongly expressed myofibroblast markers (Acta2 and Tagln) as well as Inhba.
claims.source: In addition, quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis of cells sorted from day 5 callus verified that Cd34+ cells highly expressed MPC markers including Cd34, Ly6a, Cd248, and Clec3b, whereas Cd34− cells more strongly expressed myofibroblast markers (Acta2 and Tagln) as well as Inhba (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3E showing expression of myofibroblast markers and Inhba in sorted Cd34− cells.

claims.claim: Many Td+ cells were positive for both αSMA and Activin A at day 5 post-fracture.
claims.source: Lastly, immunohistochemistry (IHC) on day 5 fractures from Col2/Td mice revealed that many Td+ cells were positive for both αSMA and Activin A (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 3F showing co-localization of αSMA and Activin A in Td+ cells.

claims.claim: Double positive cells for αSMA and Activin A included not only progenitors but also early chondrocytes.
claims.source: Those double positive cells included not only progenitors (Figure 3Fa) but also early chondrocytes (Figure 3Fb).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 3F showing double positive cells in different locations.

claims.claim: Activin A treatment stimulated cell proliferation in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor cultures.
claims.source: Cell number analysis on day 3 indicated that Activin A treatment did stimulate cell proliferation, whereas treatment with nActA.AB inhibited it (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 4A showing increased cell numbers with Activin A treatment.

claims.claim: Treatment with nActA.AB inhibited cell proliferation in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor cultures.
claims.source: Cell number analysis on day 3 indicated that Activin A treatment did stimulate cell proliferation, whereas treatment with nActA.AB inhibited it (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 4A showing decreased cell numbers with nActA.AB treatment.

claims.claim: Activin A treatment up-regulated the levels of expression of myofibroblastic cell markers including αSMA/Acta2 and Tagln.
claims.source: Remarkably, Activin A treatment up-regulated the levels of expression of myofibroblastic cell markers including αSMA/Acta2 (Figure 4B, C) and Tagln (Figure 4C)
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 4B and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4C showing increased expression of myofibroblast markers.

claims.claim: Treatment with recombinant TGF-β1 promoted myofibroblast development in periosteal cell cultures.
claims.source: Remarkably, Activin A treatment up-regulated the levels of expression of myofibroblastic cell markers including αSMA/Acta2 (Figure 4B, C) and Tagln (Figure 4C) as did treatment with recombinant TGF-β1 which is known for its ability to promote myofibroblast development (Wynn, 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 4B and citation to Wynn, 2008.

claims.claim: Activin A treatment stimulated chondrogenesis in periosteal cell cultures as revealed by strong alcian blue staining and higher expression of cartilage markers Col2a1, Acan, and Sox9.
claims.source: The treatment did stimulate chondrogenesis versus control cultures as revealed by strong alcian blue staining and higher expression of such cartilage markers as Col2a1, Acan, and Sox9 (Figure 4D, E).
claims.evidence: Supported by alcian blue staining in Figure 4D and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4E showing increased expression of chondrogenic markers.

claims.claim: Activin A treatment did not appreciably enhance osteogenic differentiation in periosteal cell cultures.
claims.source: Activin A treatment did not appreciably enhance osteogenic differentiation (Figure 4F, G).
claims.evidence: Supported by alizarin red staining in Figure 4F and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4G showing no significant increase in osteogenic markers.

claims.claim: nActA.AB treatment inhibited both osteogenesis and chondrogenesis in periosteal cell cultures.
claims.source: However, nActA.AB treatment did inhibit both osteogenesis and chondrogenesis (Figure 4D–G).
claims.evidence: Supported by alcian blue staining, alizarin red staining, and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4D-G showing decreased differentiation markers.

claims.claim: Endogenous and exogenous Activin A acts to promote chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation in periosteal progenitors.
claims.source: Thus, endogenous and exogenous Activin A acts to promote chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation in periosteal progenitors.
claims.evidence: Based on in vitro differentiation assays showing effects of Activin A treatment and neutralizing antibody on chondrogenesis and osteogenesis.

claims.claim: nActA.AB administration significantly reduced overall callus size and cartilage and bone areas at all time points post fracture (5, 7, 10, and 14 days) compared to isotype antibody controls.
claims.source: Histochemical analysis clearly showed that nActA.AB administration significantly reduced overall callus size and cartilage and bone areas at all time points post fracture (5, 7, 10, and 14 days) compared to isotype antibody controls (Figure 5A, B).
claims.evidence: Supported by Safranin O/Fast green staining images in Figure 5A and quantification in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Changes in callus volume and bone volume after nActA.AB treatment were verified by μCT analysis.
claims.source: The changes in callus volume and bone volume were verified by micro-computed tomography (μCT) analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT images and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: By 6 weeks, tibial fractures in the control group were all bridged, indicating successful recovery, but those in the nActA.AB treatment group were lagging, leading to a decrease in fracture healing score.
claims.source: By 6 weeks in the control group, the tibial fractures were all bridged, indicating a successful recovery but those in the nActA.AB treatment group were lagging, leading to a decrease in fracture healing score (Figure 5C, p = 0.006).
claims.evidence: Supported by fracture healing score data in Figure 5C showing statistically significant difference.

claims.claim: Three-point bending analysis revealed 44.4%, 35.0%, and 29.0% reductions in energy to failure, stiffness, and peak load, respectively, in fractured tibias from nActA.AB- versus isotype-treated mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, three-point bending analysis revealed 44.4%, 35.0%, and 29.0% reductions in energy to failure, stiffness, and peak load, respectively, in fractured tibias from nActA.AB- versus isotype-treated mice (Figure 5D), all statistically significant.
claims.evidence: Supported by mechanical testing data in Figure 5D showing statistically significant reductions in mechanical properties.

claims.claim: At day 7 post fracture, nActA.AB administration reduced the number of cells positive for phosphorylated SMAD2 (pSMAD2).
claims.source: At day 7 post fracture, nActA.AB administration reduced the number of cells positive for phosphorylated SMAD2 (pSMAD2) through which Activin A normally signals intracellularly (Pangas and Woodruff, 2000), suggesting the effectiveness of neutralizing antibody treatment (Figure 5E, F).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification in Figure 5E and F showing reduced pSMAD2+ cells.

claims.claim: The number of PPCs positive for αSMA and the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within PPC population were significantly decreased after nActA.AB administration.
claims.source: Interestingly, the number of PPCs positive for αSMA and the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within PPC population were significantly decreased, while the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within non-PPCs remained the same.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 5F showing differential effects on αSMA+ versus αSMA− populations.

claims.claim: The percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within non-PPCs remained the same after nActA.AB administration.
claims.source: Interestingly, the number of PPCs positive for αSMA and the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within PPC population were significantly decreased, while the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within non-PPCs remained the same.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 5F showing no change in pSMAD2+ cells within αSMA− population.

claims.claim: nActA.AB administration reduced gene expression of Acta2 and Inhba in fracture callus.
claims.source: These data were further con firmed by reduced gene expression of Acta2 and Inhba in fracture callus after nActA.AB administration (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5G showing reduced expression of Acta2 and Inhba.

claims.claim: PPCs were the primary responsive cell type to Activin A in early fracture.
claims.source: Taken together, our results clearly suggest that the PPCs were the primary responsive cell type to Activin A in early fracture
claims.evidence: Based on differential response to nActA.AB treatment between αSMA+ and αSMA− populations shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Systemic interference of Activin A action by nActA.AB treatment impaired fracture healing.
claims.source: Taken together, our results clearly suggest that the PPCs were the primary responsive cell type to Activin A in early fracture and that systemic interference of Activin A action by nActA.AB treatment impaired fracture healing.
claims.evidence: Based on comprehensive data showing reduced callus formation, mechanical properties, and healing scores after nActA.AB treatment.

claims.claim: Trabecular and cortical bone structure was essentially identical in nActA.AB- and control isotype-treated mice in contralateral, uninjured tibiae.
claims.source: We also examined contralateral, uninjured tibiae in all mice above and asked whether Activin A normally regulates bone homeostasis. µCT scanning showed that trabecular and cortical bone structure was essentially identical in nActA.AB- and control isotype-treated mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT analysis of uninjured femurs in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing no significant differences in bone parameters.

claims.claim: Activin A does not have major homeostatic roles in bone, at least within the time frame of the studies.
claims.source: µCT scanning showed that trabecular and cortical bone structure was essentially identical in nActA.AB- and control isotype-treated mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that Activin A does not have major homeostatic roles, at least within the time frame of our studies.
claims.evidence: Based on μCT analysis showing no differences in bone structure in uninjured bones after nActA.AB treatment.

claims.claim: Exogenous Activin A implantation increased callus size and cartilage and bone areas at each time point (5, 14, and 28 days) in both 2-month-old and 20-month-old mice.
claims.source: Notably, exogenous Activin A implantation had clearly increased callus size and cartilage and bone areas at each time point and in both age groups, based on histochemistry (Figure 6A, B) and μCT imaging (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by Safranin O/Fast green staining in Figure 6A, quantification in Figure 6B, and μCT images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Activin A implantation elicited a major increase in the number of mesenchymal cells positive for pSMAD2 and αSMA in fracture calluses of young mice at day 5 post fracture.
claims.source: IHC revealed that Activin A implantation had elicited a major increase in the number of mesenchymal cells positive for pSMAD2 and αSMA and the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within αSMA+ population (but not within αSMA− population) in fracture calluses of young mice at day 5 post fracture (Figure 6C, D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification in Figure 6C and D.

claims.claim: Activin A implantation increased the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within αSMA+ population but not within αSMA− population.
claims.source: IHC revealed that Activin A implantation had elicited a major increase in the number of mesenchymal cells positive for pSMAD2 and αSMA and the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within αSMA+ population (but not within αSMA− population) in fracture calluses of young mice at day 5 post fracture (Figure 6C, D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 6D showing differential effects on αSMA+ versus αSMA− populations.

claims.claim: Overall healing scores were significantly increased in both young and old mice at 6 weeks post fracture after Activin A implantation.
claims.source: Importantly, overall healing scores were significantly increased in both young and old mice at 6 weeks post fracture (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Supported by fracture healing score data in Figure 6E showing statistically significant increases.

claims.claim: Mechanical testing revealed that energy to failure, stiffness, and peak load were all significantly increased by Activin A implantation in 20-month-old mice.
claims.source: Mechanical testing revealed that energy to failure, stiffness, and peak load were all significantly increased by Activin A implantation in 20-month-old mice (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Supported by mechanical testing data in Figure 6F showing statistically significant increases in mechanical properties for 20-month-old mice.

claims.claim: Young mice had stronger bone than old mice with increased stiffness and peak load.
claims.source: In line with previous reports (Liu et al., 2022), young mice had stronger bone than old mice with increased stiffness and peak load.

results.result: Activin A expression is dramatically upregulated during fracture healing in both mice and humans. Immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry show minimal Activin A in intact bones but abundant expression in fibroblastic cells and chondrocytes within fracture callus by day 5 post-injury. Human specimens show nearly threefold increase in INHBA mRNA at fracture sites.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary approaches (immunofluorescence, immunohistochemistry, qRT-PCR) consistently demonstrate increased Activin A expression after fracture in both mouse and human samples (C1, C11-C16). The data show appropriate controls (intact vs. fractured tissue) and quantitative validation (C12). The spatiotemporal characterization is well-documented with representative images.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-sequencing identifies a novel proliferative progenitor cell (PPC) population that rapidly expands after fracture and occupies a central position in developmental trajectories leading to both chondrocytes and osteoblasts. PPCs are characterized by high proliferation rates and expression of stem cell markers at intermediate levels.
results.evaluation: The scRNA-seq analysis is comprehensive with appropriate quality controls (C40), adequate cell numbers across timepoints, and multiple computational approaches (trajectory analysis, RNA velocity) that converge on the same conclusion (C50-C52). The identification of PPCs as cluster 2 is supported by marker expression, proliferation analysis, and temporal dynamics (C46-C49). The Col2/Td reporter validation strengthens the findings (C32-C38).

results.result: PPCs express high levels of Inhba and exhibit a transient myofibroblast-like phenotype characterized by expression of Acta2, Tagln, and related genes. This phenotype is most prominent at day 5 post-fracture and diminishes by day 10. PPCs are the main source of Activin A in early fracture healing based on cell numbers and expression levels.
results.evaluation: GO term analysis, marker gene expression patterns, and validation by qRT-PCR and immunofluorescence consistently support the myofibroblast-like character of PPCs (C53-C57, C68-C71). The temporal dynamics are well-documented (C56). The inference that PPCs are the main Activin A source is reasonable given the comparative cell numbers and expression levels (C59-C62), though chondrocytes also contribute.

results.result: Activin A receptors are expressed in mesenchymal progenitor populations, with Acvr2a enriched in MPCs. Fracture enhances proliferation in both MPCs and PPCs, with PPCs showing higher proliferative capacity than MPCs at both baseline and after injury.
results.evaluation: Receptor expression is documented by UMAP plots (C64-C65), and proliferation differences are quantified by EdU incorporation with appropriate controls and statistical analysis (C66-C67). The data support the capacity of these cells to respond to Activin A signaling.

results.result: In vitro studies demonstrate that Activin A directly stimulates proliferation, myofibroblastic differentiation, and chondrogenesis in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor cultures. Neutralizing antibody treatment inhibits proliferation, chondrogenesis, and osteogenesis, indicating endogenous Activin A promotes these processes.
results.evaluation: The in vitro experiments include appropriate controls (vehicle, neutralizing antibody, TGF-β1 positive control) and multiple readouts (cell counts, marker expression, histological staining) (C72-C78). The complementary loss-of-function (antibody) and gain-of-function (recombinant protein) approaches strengthen the conclusions. However, the claim about direct osteogenic stimulation (C10, C77) is nuanced—exogenous Activin A did not enhance osteogenesis, but blocking endogenous Activin A inhibited it.

results.result: Systemic administration of neutralizing Activin A antibody significantly impairs fracture healing, reducing callus size, cartilage and bone formation, healing scores, and mechanical properties. The antibody preferentially affects PPCs (αSMA+ cells) as evidenced by reduced pSMAD2 signaling specifically in this population.
results.evaluation: The loss-of-function study is comprehensive with multiple complementary readouts (histology, μCT, mechanical testing, healing scores) at multiple timepoints (C80-C83). The cellular mechanism is investigated with immunofluorescence showing differential effects on αSMA+ versus αSMA- populations (C84-C86). Statistical significance is reported for key outcomes. The inference that PPCs are the primary responsive cell type is well-supported by the differential pSMAD2 response (C88).

results.result: Activin A does not have major homeostatic roles in bone under normal conditions, as neutralizing antibody treatment did not affect trabecular or cortical bone structure in uninjured contralateral limbs.
results.evaluation: The μCT analysis of uninjured bones provides appropriate negative control data showing no effect of Activin A blockade on bone homeostasis (C90). However, the caveat about timeframe (C91) is important—longer-term effects were not assessed. This supports the specificity of Activin A's role in injury response rather than maintenance.

results.result: Local implantation of recombinant Activin A at the fracture site enhances healing in both young (2-month) and aged (20-month) mice, increasing PPC numbers, pSMAD2 signaling, callus formation, and mechanical properties. The therapeutic effect is particularly robust in aged mice.
results.evaluation: The gain-of-function study complements the loss-of-function experiments with appropriate controls (vehicle) and demonstrates efficacy in both age groups (C92, C95-C96). The cellular mechanism is investigated showing increased PPCs and pSMAD2 signaling specifically in αSMA+ cells (C93-C94). The statistical significance of mechanical improvements in aged mice is particularly notable for translational potential. The non-significant trend in young mice (C98) is appropriately noted.

results.result: Activin A promotes bone regeneration via intramembranous ossification in a drill-hole model. Neutralizing antibody reduces bone formation while recombinant Activin A increases bone volume fraction in both medullary and cortical defect regions.
results.evaluation: The drill-hole model provides complementary evidence that Activin A's effects extend beyond endochondral ossification (C105). Both loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments show consistent effects on bone formation (C103-C104). The model is well-characterized with appropriate timepoints (C100-C102). This strengthens the generalizability of the findings.

results.result: PPCs represent a central developmental node in fracture healing, positioned between MPCs and differentiated cells (chondrocytes and osteoblasts) in trajectory analyses. PPCs are rare before injury but rapidly expand after fracture, representing the bulk of cells in thickened periosteum by day 5.
results.evaluation: Multiple computational approaches (Slingshot trajectory analysis, RNA velocity) independently place PPCs at the center of bifurcating developmental paths (C3, C50-C51). The temporal dynamics are well-documented showing expansion from low baseline numbers (C113-C115). The integration of computational predictions with experimental validation strengthens these conclusions.

results.result: Activin A functions as an overall regulator and stimulator of fracture repair, acting through multiple cell types and differentiation pathways. The protein's capacity to influence inflammation, progenitor proliferation, and multiple differentiation lineages positions it as a potential therapeutic with advantages over current single-pathway approaches.
results.evaluation: While the comprehensive loss-of-function and gain-of-function data strongly support Activin A's regulatory role in fracture healing (C108-C109), the broader claims about its advantages as a therapeutic (C132, C135-C136) are speculative and not directly tested. The mechanistic link to inflammation (C131) is inferred from prior literature rather than demonstrated in this study. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not fully supported by the current data.

results.result: The study builds on established knowledge about fracture healing biology, periosteal progenitor cells, and Activin A's roles in other contexts. Prior work has identified αSMA+ periosteal cells as important for healing and demonstrated Activin A's pro-chondrogenic activity and role in heterotopic ossification.
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately cite relevant prior literature (C18-C31, C106-C107) and provide context for the current work. The citations appear accurate and relevant. This represents appropriate scholarly contextualization rather than new findings.

results.result: The identified MPC and PPC populations share characteristics with previously described periosteal and fibroblast progenitor cells across multiple tissues. MPCs express markers similar to early mesenchymal progenitors in bone marrow and Pi16+ universal fibroblast progenitors. PPCs share features with injury-induced Lrrc15+ myofibroblastic cells.
results.evaluation: The comparative analysis with prior literature is thorough and well-supported by marker expression data (C121-C126). The identification of shared characteristics across tissue types (C127) is appropriately cautious. However, the lack of Mx1 expression (mentioned in text) contradicts one prior study, which is appropriately noted. This contextualizes the findings within the broader field.

results.result: Current therapeutic approaches for fracture healing are limited, with no effective and safe therapy clinically available. Existing anabolic therapies target single pathways or populations, which may limit their effectiveness. Activin A's role in inflammation may link the initial injury response to subsequent skeletal repair.
results.evaluation: The claims about limitations of current therapies are supported by appropriate citations (C133-C134). However, the speculation about Activin A linking inflammation to skeletal repair (C130) is not directly tested in this study—it's an inference based on known inflammatory roles of Activin A. This represents a reasonable hypothesis but lacks direct experimental support in the current work.
